source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and LLMs
finding: Review that maps the human metrics (phi, type-2 AUROC, meta-d', ECE) onto LLM work. It splits metacognition into sensitivity (does confidence separate right from wrong) and calibration (is the level right). Most sensitivity metrics except meta-d' are contaminated by task accuracy.
numbers: Example AUCs: GPT-3.5 token-likelihood confidence on MMLU AUC 0.778; fine-tuned GPT-4.1-mini verbal confidence on TriviaQA AUC 0.83.
quote: Most measures of metacognitive sensitivity are contaminated by type 1 accuracy
limits: Cross-model comparisons with AUROC alone are confounded by accuracy; almost no LLM paper uses meta-d'.
agent_relevance: When we compare confidence methods in our scaffold, report AUROC and ECE per question set, and note accuracy, because a better model alone raises AUROC.

source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and LLMs
finding: The review says consistency of sampled answers as a confidence signal in LLMs matches Koriat's self-consistency model of human confidence (2012). Both were developed independently.
numbers: Qualitative link only. Also notes implicit token-likelihood confidence tracks accuracy trial by trial better than verbalised confidence (citing Xiong 2024).
limits: Link is an analogy, not a test that LLMs use the same mechanism.
agent_relevance: Supports the plan to derive confidence from agreement among samples, computed by code (G5), not from the model's self-report.

source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and LLMs
finding: Human vs LLM: both overconfident, similar AUROC2 in one study (Cash et al. 2025), but that study did not control accuracy. Training in humans improves calibration but not sensitivity; fine-tuning LLMs improves both, with only partial transfer across domains.
numbers: Cash et al. 2025 and Steyvers et al. 2025a are cited, not opened by me.
limits: Secondary report of other studies.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning for confidence is out of scope (no training), so only prompt and code-side signals apply.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation (ICLR)
finding: Verbalised confidence from LLMs is overconfident and hardly separates right from wrong. GPT-4 vanilla verbalised confidence averages AUROC 62.7% across eight tasks (chance is 50%). Larger models do better, about 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
numbers: Five models (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA 2), eight datasets; average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna.
quote: LLMs tend to be overconfident when verbalizing their confidence
limits: Black-box prompting only; professional-knowledge tasks such as law stay hard.
agent_relevance: Never gate a decision on a verbalised 'I am 90% sure'. G4/G5 already point this way.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation (ICLR)
finding: Sample consistency beats verbalised confidence for failure prediction. On GSM8K with GPT-3.5, 5 sampled answers with consistency aggregation raised AUROC from 54.8% (Top-K, one sample) to 92.7%.
numbers: GPT-3.5, M=5. Averages over five datasets: single CoT verbalised ECE 24.3 AUROC 69.2; Top-K single ECE 25.0 AUROC 56.4; self-random M=5 ECE 17.3 AUROC 69.6; prompt-varied M=5 ECE 18.7 AUROC 73.0.
quote: consistency among multiple responses is more effective in improving failure prediction and calibration
limits: Gain is large on arithmetic (answers easy to match), small on Professional Law (AUROC 59-66 with M=5). Sampling gains flatten as M grows (tested M=1 to 13). Row labels in the table text extraction were partly scrambled, so the per-method averages should be rechecked against the PDF.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'confidence from consistency of samples, by code'. Use agreement rate over about 5 samples as the doubt signal (G1), not the model's own words.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation (ICLR)
finding: Calibration can be gamed and hides weak discrimination. GPT-4 on GSM8K (93.6% accuracy) gets ECE 0.064 by saying 100% for everything, which tells nothing about which answers are wrong.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-4.
limits: Shows ECE alone is a poor metric when accuracy is high.
agent_relevance: Judge any confidence signal by AUROC or within-question discrimination, not ECE alone.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation (ICLR)
finding: Adding verbalised confidence to the consistency vote helps: Pair-Rank aggregation reached ECE as low as 0.028; Avg-Conf gave the best failure prediction. Human-inspired prompts (step-by-step, top-K guesses) cut overconfidence but only partly. White-box vs black-box gap is small.
numbers: White-box AUROC 0.605 vs black-box 0.522 on one comparison; no single method won everywhere.
limits: Authors say no technique consistently beat the others.
agent_relevance: Black-box methods are close enough to white-box that a closed-model agent loses little.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false questions when the format is right. For open answers, ask the model to propose an answer and then give P(True). P(True) improves when the model sees several of its own samples first.
numbers: Anthropic models up to 52B; many tasks (TriviaQA, GSM8K, code, MMLU). P(IK) classifier AUROC rises with model size; training on all tasks helps all tasks.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions
limits: Calibration fails on new tasks for P(IK) and when formats change (e.g. 'none of the above' option).
agent_relevance: Shows sample-then-judge works. Showing the model its own samples before judging is a consistency-style signal.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK), the chance that the model knows the answer before answering, was trained as a head. It rises in the right way when relevant source text or hints are added to the context.
numbers: Example: P(IK) for a Wikipedia-article question rose from about 18% (52B, no article) to 78% with it.
limits: Trained head, so not available to a no-training scaffold.
agent_relevance: Idea of asking before attempting maps to a cheap 'can I do this?' check, but would need training to be reliable.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration: Eliciting Calibrated Confidence from RLHF Language Models
finding: For RLHF chat models, verbalised confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for top-k guesses with probabilities in one turn is best, often cutting ECE by a relative 50% or more.
numbers: TriviaQA with gpt-3.5-turbo: label probability ECE 0.140, AUC 0.869; verbalised one-stage top-1 ECE 0.068, AUC 0.879; top-2 ECE 0.050, AUC 0.894. SciQ: label prob ECE 0.256 vs verbalised top-4 ECE 0.065. ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2 tested.
limits: On TruthfulQA all methods are poor (AUC 0.38-0.55, below 0.5 for some). Temperature scaling changes rankings. Contradicts Xiong 2024 on whether verbal beats logits for discrimination.
agent_relevance: 'Consider the opposite' (top-k guesses) is a cheap debiasing prompt, in line with human debiasing research.

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation (ICLR)
finding: Semantic entropy clusters sampled answers by meaning (bidirectional entailment) and takes entropy over meaning clusters. It predicts correctness better than token-sequence entropy, lexical similarity, and p(True), and the gap grows with model size.
numbers: TriviaQA and CoQA, OPT models up to 30B. AUROC axes run 0.65 to 0.85 with semantic entropy highest at the largest size (exact values not recorded).
limits: Needs an entailment model; accuracy and answer diversity trade off (temperature choice matters).
agent_relevance: Our grouping of samples by meaning, done by code or a small checker, is the right way to count 'agreement' for free-text answers (G5).

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation (ICLR)
finding: Sampling temperature has two competing effects: higher temperature gives more diverse answers (better uncertainty signal) but lower accuracy. Best AUROC sits at a middle value.
numbers: Section 6 ablations on sampling method and temperature.
limits: Specific to the models tested.
agent_relevance: Choose a moderate temperature for the confidence samples, separate from the final-answer sample.

source: Farquhar et al. (2024) Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy (Nature)
finding: Extension of semantic entropy to longer text and more models; reported as beating naive entropy and embedding baselines for flagging confabulations.
numbers: Not opened. From memory, average AUROC about 0.79 vs 0.69 for naive entropy; verify before use.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the 'verify later' list.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know (Nature Machine Intelligence)
finding: There is a calibration gap and a discrimination gap between what the LLM knows and what users believe. With default explanations, users' confidence in the LLM answer is much worse calibrated than the model's own, and barely tells right from wrong.
numbers: Model confidence AUC: GPT-3.5 0.751, PaLM2 0.746 (multiple choice), GPT-4o 0.781 (short answer). Human AUC from default explanations: 0.589 and 0.602 (multiple choice), 0.592 (short answer). Mean participant AUC across Exp 2a-c: 0.54 (long) and 0.57.
quote: Participants overestimate LLM accuracy; explanation length drives it.
limits: Online participants; MMLU-style items.
agent_relevance: If a human reads our agent's output, the agent's own confidence must be surfaced in a form people use; long confident-sounding text misleads.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know (Nature Machine Intelligence)
finding: Tuning the explanation wording to the model's real confidence narrows both gaps, though a gap remains.
numbers: Gap in ECE and AUC narrowed vs baseline explanations (Figures 2-3). Multiple-choice LLM confidence overconfident; short-answer LLM confidence slightly underconfident.
limits: Narrowed, not closed; length of explanation also mattered.
agent_relevance: Report uncertainty in the final answer in matching wording; do not pad.

source: Sun, Li, Wang & Goette (2025) Large Language Models are overconfident and amplify human bias
finding: Five LLMs overestimate the chance their answers are right by 20% (GPT o1) to 60% (GPT 3.5) on algorithmically built reasoning problems. Humans on the same task: 66% accuracy, think 70%, only 4 points over.
numbers: Overconfidence gap p<0.001 per model. For humans sure at 100%, accuracy was 81%.
quote: LLM bias increases sharply relative to humans if they become less sure
limits: Bias in LLMs rises sharply when they are less sure; a 10% drop in confidence goes with about 25% drop in accuracy for GPT-4o and o1, about 13% for Llama 3.1.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models (o1) are less overconfident than GPT-3.5, but still not calibrated; do not trust self-reported certainty.

source: Sun, Li, Wang & Goette (2025) Large Language Models are overconfident and amplify human bias
finding: Showing LLM answers to humans raises their accuracy but also their overconfidence: bias rises by 7.0 points in the LLM Answer condition, and confidence display adds 4.2 to 7.6 points.
numbers: Human experiment; overconfidence more than doubles with LLM input vs a baseline of about 4%.
limits: Specific incentive-compatible design.
agent_relevance: Confidence from our agent should be shown with care, as it can transfer false certainty to the reader.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weighting each sampled answer by model-given confidence needs about 40% fewer samples than plain majority vote to match it. With P(True) confidence the cost reduction is 41% (budget 5) and 46% (budget 10).
numbers: Nine models, four datasets. Cost reduction at budget 10: verbal binary 10%, verbal 1-100 30%, response probability 31%, P(True) 46%. Accuracy gains small, 0.2 to 1.6 points.
limits: Gains depend on confidence method; within-question normalisation matters for P(True) (32% to 46%).
agent_relevance: Our G4/G5 says no extremising votes; CISC is a code-side weighted vote and could be tested as a cheaper vote, not as proof.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: New metric, within-question discrimination (WQD): given two answers to the same question, does the higher confidence one tend to be the correct one. The usual between-question metrics are poor predictors of voting gain.
numbers: WQD: verbal binary 52.2%, verbal 0-100 56.1%, response probability 59.0%, P(True) 62.3%. Their ECE-t: 0.005, 0.046, 0.090, 0.030.
limits: Best ECE did not give best WQD (verbal binary has lowest ECE, near-chance WQD).
agent_relevance: Right metric for picking among our own samples. Adopt WQD to test any confidence signal in the loop.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Internal token confidence over sliding groups of tokens (not the whole trace average) filters weak reasoning traces. Offline, DeepConf@512 reaches 99.9% on AIME 2025 with GPT-OSS-120B vs 97.0% majority vote and 91.8% single sample.
numbers: Online mode stops low-confidence traces early and cuts generated tokens by up to 84.7%. Group window 1024 or 2048 tokens.
quote: reduces token generation by up to 84.7% compared to standard parallel thinking
limits: Needs token log-probs, so open-weight or logprob-exposing APIs; confidence is the model's internal signal and may reward fluent wrong traces.
agent_relevance: A trace-quality signal from logprobs is possible if we host the model. Otherwise use sample agreement.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Whole-trace average confidence hides local breakdowns; low-confidence tokens such as 'wait', 'however', 'think again' mark reasoning breakdowns, so a local group signal is better.
numbers: Qualitative plus ablations on average vs group vs tail confidence.
limits: Authors' own benchmarks (AIME, HMMT, BRUMO, GPQA).
agent_relevance: Echoes our G1: doubt on a signal. A local low-confidence stretch is a candidate impasse signal.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (NeurIPS)
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration. About 1000 graded examples with LoRA fine-tuning beat baselines. Sampling methods give decent calibration but weak discrimination; verbal elicitation discriminates fairly but calibrates badly even after temperature scaling.
numbers: MMLU multiple choice and open-ended; ECE does not improve with base-model ability, AUROC improves slightly.
quote: prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration
limits: Needs training; not used by a no-training scaffold. Partly disagrees with Xiong 2024 (who found sampling better at discrimination on GSM8K).
agent_relevance: Confirms that no single cheap signal both calibrates and discriminates; combine them in code.

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: First paper to show a finetuned GPT-3 can state calibrated confidence in words and numbers on CalibratedMath. The calibration is not just copied logits and survives some distribution shift.
numbers: CalibratedMath suite; verbalised and indirect-logit probabilities both generalise under shift; compared to answer-logit baseline.
limits: Needs fine-tuning; arithmetic only.
agent_relevance: Background to later prompt-only work (Tian, Xiong).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning (ICLR)
finding: Sample many reasoning paths and take the most common answer. Large gains over greedy chain of thought. The agreement rate of the vote correlates with accuracy, so it also serves as a confidence signal.
numbers: GSM8K +17.9 (code-davinci-002 78.0), SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, AddSub +1.8, MultiArith +4.6/+3.8. Figure 5: consistency vs accuracy highly correlated on GSM8K.
quote: aggregated answer) is highly correlated with accuracy
limits: Probability-weighted voting (unnormalised or length-normalised) was no better than a simple majority because the path probabilities were nearly equal.
agent_relevance: Founding method behind 'confidence from consistency'. Samples share one model and so are not independent (G4); agreement is a hint, not proof.

source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience)
finding: Human source for meta-d' and M-ratio (meta-d'/d'): a bias-free sensitivity measure in the same units as task d'. Not opened; described as cited by Steyvers & Peters (opened).
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Assumes an equal-variance signal detection model with binary decisions; LLM multi-answer tasks need a conversion.
agent_relevance: If we want an accuracy-free confidence score for the agent, meta-d' or M-ratio is the human-literature answer; needs a binary-decision framing.

source: Koriat (2012) The self-consistency model of subjective confidence (Psychological Review)
finding: Human model: confidence follows the consistency among representations the person samples. Cited as the human parallel to sample-agreement confidence in LLMs. Not opened; no numbers recorded.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Mechanism in humans is debated; LLM agreement is only an analogy.
agent_relevance: Gives the human warrant for the consistency-of-samples design.

source: Griot et al. (2025) Large language models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning (Nature Communications)
finding: Cited by Steyvers & Peters as evidence that LLMs struggle to recognise gaps in their knowledge in medical questions. Not opened.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Secondary mention only.
agent_relevance: A warning that self-knowledge may fail in specialist areas.
